answers.text:
This is the term Seth introduces here for the specific assumption he's setting out to challenge for the rest of the essay. As he defines it in this same passage, it is the philosophical view that consciousness is a matter of computation. More specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise.

The key word is "sufficient": on this view, if you run the right program — the right pattern of information-processing — on any physical system capable of running it, consciousness will show up, regardless of what that system is made of. It's a specific, stronger claim than just "the brain's organization matters for the mind" (which Seth later calls functionalism-in-general); computational functionalism narrows that down to say the relevant organization is computational, and typically means computational in the Turing-machine sense — the kind of step-by-step, substrate-independent symbol manipulation that ordinary digital computers do.

Seth flags this as usually going unexamined: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all. He treats it as the load-bearing premise beneath the whole "conscious AI is coming" narrative, and says that if it's false, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with. The rest of the essay's four-part argument (brains aren't computers, other non-computational dynamics may matter, life itself may matter, and simulation isn't instantiation) is essentially a sustained case against this one assumption.

answers.asked: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.
answers.text:
This is naming and flagging the assumption that the whole essay is built around challenging. The sentence right before it in the article states the assumption itself: that the very idea of conscious AI rests on the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation... that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Computational functionalism is the philosophical label for that view — the position that if you run the right kind of information-processing, consciousness follows, regardless of what the system is physically made of.

The point of the sentence you've selected is about how invisible this assumption has become. It isn't attacking the idea yet — Seth is setting up why it needs attacking at all: because it's usually treated as obvious rather than as a claim that could be false. He goes on to say exactly this: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with. So this passage functions as a hinge. Everything before it in the essay has been about the psychological biases that make people leap to "AI is conscious." Everything after it (the four arguments — brains aren't computers, other games in town, life matters, simulation isn't instantiation) is Seth's attempt to show that this specific assumption, computational functionalism, is not a neutral starting point but a substantive and contestable claim that most conversations about machine consciousness smuggle in without ever stating it.

answers.asked: What does "computational functionalism" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In the piece, computational functionalism is defined as the assumption that consciousness is a matter of computation — that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise, and Seth calls it out as a premise so familiar that people forget it is one [spya-wepmnr]. He frames it as the load-bearing assumption under the whole "conscious AI" question: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with [spya-wepmnr].

It matters to the argument because the rest of the essay is essentially a case against this one assumption. Seth says he will summarize four related arguments that undermine the idea that computation, at least of the sort implemented in standard digital computers, is sufficient for consciousness [spya-cv97j7] — that brains aren't computers in the relevant sense, that plenty of brain-relevant dynamics (continuous, stochastic, embodied processes) fall outside Turing-style computation, that being alive may itself be necessary for consciousness, and that simulating a process is not the same as instantiating it. Each of these is aimed squarely at computational functionalism, and he later notes their cumulative effect: Computational functionalism — the claim that (algorithmic) computation is sufficient for consciousness — is a very strong assumption that looks increasingly shaky as the many and deep differences between brains and (standard digital) computers come into view [spya-ymbpwn]. He also flags it as usually silent even where it's doing the most work — for instance in Bostrom's simulation argument, where it is telling that he notes one necessary assumption, and then just takes it as a given… the assumption that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious" [spya-xdy4fe]. So the term names the single hidden hinge that every hope (or fear) of conscious AI swings on, and the whole middle section of the essay is Seth's attempt to show that hinge is weaker than people assume.

Within the passage, the word names the specific process just described: that even a single neuron is "a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence." The article itself glosses the word as coming "from the Greek for 'self-production'" and calls it "arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems." So in plain terms: a living cell doesn't just process inputs and outputs the way a computer does — it is continuously building and repairing the very physical stuff that makes it what it is. A neuron isn't just running a program; it's also busy keeping itself alive.

This detail is doing specific work in Seth's larger argument that brains are not computers. He's building toward the claim that in a computer you can cleanly separate the software (what it does) from the hardware (what it's made of), but in a brain you cannot make that separation, because the very material of a neuron is bound up in sustaining its own existence. That's why the next sentences move straight to saying brains are "the kinds of things for which it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are." Autopoiesis is the concept that anchors that claim in biology rather than leaving it as loose metaphor.

Though the article doesn't say so, the term itself was coined in the early 1970s by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to describe exactly this kind of self-maintaining, self-producing organization found in living cells — it's a fairly standard piece of vocabulary in theoretical biology and in the "4E cognitive science" tradition the essay gestures toward later, and it's part of why some philosophers (Searle's biological naturalism, which Seth discusses shortly after) treat being alive, not just being organized the right way, as relevant to consciousness.

answers.asked: (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)
answers.text:
Autopoiesis is a concept coined by Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela in the early 1970s to define what makes something alive. The core idea is that a living system is one that continuously produces and maintains its own components and its own boundary (like a cell membrane) through its own internal processes, rather than being built or maintained by something outside it. A living cell isn't just a structure that happens to persist; it is constantly rebuilding itself from the inside, using its own activity to regenerate the very parts and conditions that keep it existing as a distinct entity. This is different from something like a car engine, which does work but doesn't manufacture and repair its own parts as a condition of its own existence.

In the passage, the article uses this idea right after pointing out that a single neuron is "a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence." Autopoiesis names that self-maintaining activity, and the article treats it as "a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems" — the Greek roots literally meaning "self-production."

This matters for Seth's larger argument because it's one of the properties that separates a brain from a computer. A computer's hardware doesn't need to keep regenerating itself in order to keep running the software; a neuron's "hardware" (its molecular and metabolic machinery) is inseparable from what it does, because that machinery is continually rebuilding itself. That's part of the case, developed a few paragraphs later, that brains can't be cleanly split into software and hardware the way computers can — and therefore that simply running the right algorithm on silicon may not be enough to produce consciousness.

answers.asked: What does "autopoiesis" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
The article defines it directly: autopoiesis is "self-production," from the Greek — the process by which even a single neuron is "busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence," and the piece calls it "arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems" [spya-cf8rt8].

Why it matters: it does two jobs in the argument. First, in the "Brains Are Not Computers" section, it's evidence for why brains resist the clean software/hardware split that Turing computation depends on — a computer's hardware just runs the program, but a neuron's own physical activity is continuously producing and repairing the very thing that does the "computing." That is part of why the piece says "the idea of the brain as a meat-based (universal) Turing machine rests precisely on this sharp separation of scales, on the substrate independence that motivated Turing's definition in the first place", and why breaking that separation counts as evidence against computational functionalism [spya-p4vmm0].

Second, it resurfaces in the "Life Matters" section as the link between biology and consciousness itself: the essay argues "This drive to stay alive doesn't bottom out anywhere in particular. It reaches deep into the interior of each cell, into the molecular furnaces of metabolism. Within these whirls of metabolic activity, the ubiquitous process of prediction error minimization becomes inseparable from the materiality of life itself." It then draws "A mathematical line... directly from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material all the way to the Bayesian best-guessing that underpins our perceptual experiences of the world and of the self."

So autopoiesis is doing double duty: it's a concrete reason brains can't be cleanly abstracted into software running on hardware, and it's the biological thread the essay uses to connect being alive to having conscious experience — the basis for the "biological naturalism" position the whole piece is building toward.
